prompt: What is the atomic packing factor of a face-centred cubic (FCC) crystal?
explanation: FCC and HCP are both close-packed structures with packing efficiency 74 %, the highest possible for identical hard spheres. BCC is 68 %, simple cubic is 52 %, and 100 % packing is geometrically impossible for spheres.

prompt: FCC and HCP both achieve the maximum packing density. What distinguishes them?
options: Different stacking sequences of close-packed planes — ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP
correctAnswer: Different stacking sequences of close-packed planes — ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP
explanation: Both structures are built from the same close-packed planes; they differ only in how those planes stack. FCC uses an ABCABC repeat (periodic in 3 layers); HCP uses ABAB (periodic in 2 layers). The local coordination is identical (12 nearest neighbours), but bulk properties differ because of the global symmetry difference.

prompt: Which of the following metals has a body-centred cubic structure at room temperature?
explanation: α-Iron (the room-temperature ferrite phase) is BCC. Above 912 °C it transforms to FCC γ-iron (austenite). Copper, aluminium, and gold are all FCC. The BCC → FCC transformation in iron is at the heart of steel heat treatment.

prompt: Bragg's law for X-ray diffraction is nλ = 2d sin _____.
explanation: Bragg's law gives constructive interference when nλ = 2d sinθ, where d is the spacing between crystal planes and θ is the glancing angle. Each crystal lattice produces a unique pattern of diffraction peaks — a fingerprint that identifies the structure.

prompt: Match each crystal type to a typical example:
explanation: Each structure family is associated with a class of properties. Diamond cubic underlies semiconductors. Rock salt is the prototype ionic crystal. Perovskite hosts ferroelectrics, superconductors, and modern halide solar cells.

prompt: How many distinct three-dimensional Bravais lattices exist?
explanation: Bravais (1850) showed there are exactly 14 distinct lattices in three dimensions, organised into 7 crystal systems and 4 centring types. Adding a basis of atoms in different orientations multiplies into the 230 space groups, but the underlying lattice geometry has only 14 cases.

prompt: A plane intercepts the cubic axes at (1, 1, ∞). Its Miller indices are:
explanation: Take reciprocals of the intercepts (1, 1, ∞) → (1, 1, 0). After clearing fractions (none needed) the Miller indices are (110). This plane cuts diagonally across two cube faces and is parallel to the third axis.

prompt: Why are FCC metals (Cu, Al, Au) generally more ductile at room temperature than HCP metals (Ti, Mg, Zn)?
options: FCC metals are softer at the atomic scale
FCC has 12 active slip systems on close-packed planes; HCP has only the basal plane easily activated
FCC and HCP have the same ductility
correctAnswer: FCC has 12 active slip systems on close-packed planes; HCP has only the basal plane easily activated
explanation: Plastic deformation requires multiple independent slip systems. FCC offers twelve combinations of {111} planes and ⟨110⟩ directions, allowing deformation in any orientation. HCP normally only uses the basal {0001} plane, leaving fewer independent systems and limited room-temperature ductility.

prompt: The cubic plane that contains all three cube body diagonals — passing through three corners of the unit cell — has Miller indices (_____).
explanation: The (111) plane intercepts each axis at 1, giving reciprocals (1,1,1). It is the close-packed plane in FCC crystals — the same family of planes that forms the basis of every FCC slip system.

prompt: Match each crystal system to a key constraint on its unit cell:

pairs.right: a = b ≠ c, two angles 90° and one 120°

explanation: Each crystal system is defined by symmetry constraints on the unit cell. Cubic has the highest symmetry (every direction equivalent); triclinic has the least, with no constrained edges or angles. The seven crystal systems are exhaustive — every periodic crystal fits into one.

prompt: Why does any crystal at finite temperature contain some equilibrium concentration of vacancies?
options: Configurational entropy makes vacancies thermodynamically favourable, so the free energy minimum sits at a non-zero defect concentration
Vacancies are required for X-ray diffraction
correctAnswer: Configurational entropy makes vacancies thermodynamically favourable, so the free energy minimum sits at a non-zero defect concentration
explanation: Each vacancy costs an enthalpy ΔH_v but adds k_B ln(arrangements) of entropy. Minimising free energy F = U − TS gives an equilibrium fraction n_v/N ≈ exp(−ΔH_v / k_B T) — non-zero at any finite T.

prompt: Carbon dissolved in iron sits in:
options: Interstitial sites — squeezed between iron atoms
correctAnswer: Interstitial sites — squeezed between iron atoms
explanation: Carbon (atomic radius ~0.7 Å) is small enough to occupy interstitial holes in the iron lattice rather than replacing host atoms. Interstitial carbon distorts the lattice and is the central player in the strengthening of all carbon steels.

prompt: A Schottky defect in an ionic crystal consists of:
options: A paired cation vacancy and anion vacancy that preserves charge neutrality
correctAnswer: A paired cation vacancy and anion vacancy that preserves charge neutrality
explanation: In ionic crystals individual vacancies would unbalance charge. Schottky pairs (cation vacancy + anion vacancy) and Frenkel pairs (interstitial + vacancy of the same ion) are the standard ways to introduce point defects while keeping the bulk neutral.

prompt: Diffusion in solids follows an Arrhenius law D = D₀ exp(−Q / k_B T), where Q is the _____ energy.
explanation: Q is the activation energy for an atom to hop between lattice sites — for example, into a neighbouring vacancy. Low temperatures freeze diffusion almost completely; small temperature increases produce exponential changes in atomic mobility.

prompt: Match each material phenomenon to the point defect responsible:
explanation: Each example is dominated by one type of point defect. Substitutional dopants control electronic properties of semiconductors. Interstitials drive solid-solution strengthening of steels. Vacancies enable diffusion — which underlies every solid-state heat treatment.

prompt: Why does a real copper wire yield at far lower stress than an idealised perfect copper crystal?
options: Plastic flow proceeds by dislocation motion — slip occurs one bond at a time, requiring far less stress than simultaneously breaking every bond on a slip plane
Copper crystals are weak by nature
correctAnswer: Plastic flow proceeds by dislocation motion — slip occurs one bond at a time, requiring far less stress than simultaneously breaking every bond on a slip plane
explanation: The ideal calculation gives ~G/10 (~5 GPa for copper), but real copper yields at ~50 MPa — 100× less. Dislocations propagate slip locally, like a caterpillar moving by passing a hump along its body. Taylor, Orowan, and Polanyi proposed this in 1934.

prompt: In an edge dislocation, the Burgers vector is:
explanation: An edge dislocation has its Burgers vector perpendicular to the dislocation line. A screw dislocation has its Burgers vector parallel to the line. Real dislocations are usually mixed loops with both characters along their length, but the Burgers vector remains constant along any single dislocation.

prompt: The Hall-Petch relation σ_y = σ_0 + k/√d describes how yield strength depends on:
options: Grain size — smaller grains give higher strength
correctAnswer: Grain size — smaller grains give higher strength
explanation: Hall-Petch ties yield stress to grain size d: smaller grains mean more grain boundary area per unit volume, more obstacles per unit dislocation path, and higher yield strength. Severe plastic deformation processes (ECAP, HPT) produce sub-micron grains and exploit this effect for very strong metals.

prompt: Cold-rolling copper increases its yield strength because plastic deformation increases the dislocation density — a phenomenon called _____ hardening.
explanation: Cold work multiplies dislocations until they tangle and obstruct each other, raising the stress required for further plastic flow. Cold-rolled copper can be many times stronger than annealed copper but is correspondingly less ductile.

prompt: Match each strengthening mechanism to its primary obstacle to dislocation motion:
explanation: Each route to strength obstructs dislocations differently. Solid-solution strengthening uses point-defect stress fields. Precipitation hardening uses fine particles (e.g. duralumin's Cu-Al precipitates). Grain refinement uses Hall-Petch behaviour. Real engineering alloys combine all three.

prompt: Most engineering metals are polycrystalline, meaning they consist of:
options: Many small crystallites (grains) with different orientations, separated by grain boundaries
correctAnswer: Many small crystallites (grains) with different orientations, separated by grain boundaries
explanation: Polycrystalline metals are aggregates of microscopic grains, typically 1–100 µm across, each with a different crystallographic orientation. The thin disordered region where grains meet is a grain boundary, with its own free energy and kinetic behaviour.

prompt: Why does annealing soften a heavily worked metal?
options: Annealing converts the metal to a different element
Annealing relieves residual stresses, allows recovery of dislocation tangles, and grows new strain-free grains, reducing dislocation density
correctAnswer: Annealing relieves residual stresses, allows recovery of dislocation tangles, and grows new strain-free grains, reducing dislocation density
explanation: Cold work raises dislocation density and stored energy. Annealing supplies thermal activation: dislocations rearrange, new low-defect grains nucleate (recrystallisation), and grains grow. The result is a lower dislocation density and a softer, more ductile microstructure.

prompt: A twin boundary is best described as:
options: A planar defect across which the lattice is reflected as in a mirror
correctAnswer: A planar defect across which the lattice is reflected as in a mirror
explanation: Twin boundaries are mirror-symmetric planar defects. They have lower energy than typical grain boundaries because the lattice match across the plane is excellent. Annealing twins in copper and brass are common; deformation twins are an alternative to slip when slip systems are limited (e.g. HCP titanium).

prompt: Pores, oxide inclusions, and similar three-dimensional defects often act as starting points for _____ failure under cyclic loading.
explanation: Cyclic loading concentrates stress at sharp internal flaws — voids, inclusions, machining marks. Fatigue cracks usually nucleate at the largest such defect, then propagate stably until the remaining cross-section is too small to bear load. Inclusion control is therefore central to high-cycle fatigue design.

prompt: Match each defect to its dimensionality:
explanation: Defects are usefully classified by dimension: 0-D point defects (vacancies, interstitials, substitutionals), 1-D line defects (dislocations), 2-D planar defects (grain boundaries, twins, stacking faults), and 3-D volume defects (pores, inclusions, cracks). Each scale has its own characteristic effect on properties.
